coursePlan.title: Idempotent Requests
ideas: Idempotency means repeating a request leaves state unchanged

blocks.title: What Idempotency Means
blocks.body: An operation is idempotent when executing it once or multiple times leaves the target resource in the same final state. HTTP PUT replaces the resource at a URI, so repeating the exact same PUT request produces the same state.

blocks.title: Retries Over Unreliable Networks
blocks.body: When a network timeout hides the server's response, a client can safely retry an idempotent request without creating duplicate side effects.

reported.note: The opening paragraph feels slightly dry; add a motivating real-world e-commerce anecdote to improve tone and engagement.
According to RFC 9110 section 9.2.2, HTTP DELETE is also defined as idempotent and should be cited from the RFC.
Consider splitting the long sentence into two shorter sentences for better readability.

blocks.title: Idempotency Rule
blocks.body: An idempotent HTTP request never modifies any state on the server under any circumstances.

blocks.title: How PUT Works
blocks.body: HTTP PUT is an idempotent request, and its first call creates or replaces the stored resource state on the server.

reported.passage: An idempotent HTTP request never modifies any state on the server under any circumstances.
reported.note: Section 1 says an idempotent HTTP request never modifies server state, which contradicts Section 2 saying PUT is idempotent and modifies the stored resource state on the server.

authoringContext.priorKnowledge: Basic familiarity with sending JSON payloads.

coursePlan.title: Conditional Requests
actions: Send a conditional PUT with If-Match

blocks.title: Update an Order Safely
blocks.body: Use curl with an If-Match header carrying the order's current ETag to send a conditional PUT request, and verify that a stale ETag returns 412 Precondition Failed.

blocks.title: What ETag and If-Match Are
blocks.body: An ETag is an opaque version identifier returned by the server in a response header. To perform a conditional PUT with If-Match, first copy the ETag value from a GET response, then run curl -X PUT -H "If-Match: <etag>" with your JSON body; the server applies the update and returns 200 OK if the ETag matches, or rejects it with 412 Precondition Failed if another writer updated the resource first.

reported.passage: Use curl with an If-Match header carrying the order's current ETag to send a conditional PUT request, and verify that a stale ETag returns 412 Precondition Failed.
reported.note: Section 1 asks the learner to send a conditional PUT with If-Match and ETag before Section 2 defines ETag or shows how to send an If-Match header.

blocks.title: Retry Flow
blocks.body: When a client retries a payment request, it attaches the same key on each attempt. As shown in Step 4 of the companion sequence diagram above, the server replays the stored receipt instead of charging the card twice.

blocks.title: Read Committed Guarantee
blocks.body: Under Read Committed isolation, a transaction can never read uncommitted changes written by another active transaction.

blocks.title: Concurrent Walkthrough
blocks.body: In this Read Committed walkthrough, Transaction B reads Transaction A's uncommitted balance update before Transaction A commits.

reported.passage: In this Read Committed walkthrough, Transaction B reads Transaction A's uncommitted balance update before Transaction A commits.
reported.note: Section 2 contradicts Section 1: Section 1 states Read Committed never reads uncommitted changes, while Section 2 shows Transaction B reading an uncommitted balance update under Read Committed.
The heading 'Read Committed Guarantee' would sound punchier if rephrased as a question.

coursePlan.title: Safe vs Idempotent
ideas: Safe and idempotent are distinct properties

blocks.title: Safe Methods
blocks.body: HTTP GET is a safe method because it does not modify server state.

blocks.title: Idempotent Methods
blocks.body: HTTP DELETE is not safe because it removes a resource, yet it is idempotent because repeating the DELETE leaves the resource absent.

reported.passage: HTTP DELETE is not safe because it removes a resource, yet it is idempotent because repeating the DELETE leaves the resource absent.
reported.note: Section 1 and Section 2 contradict each other because Section 1 talks about not modifying state while Section 2 says DELETE modifies state and is still idempotent.

authoringContext.priorKnowledge: The learner already knows how to run basic curl commands from the terminal to send GET and POST requests.

blocks.title: Checking Liveness
blocks.body: A liveness endpoint returns HTTP 200 OK when the service process is healthy. Send a GET request to /healthz with curl and confirm the status line reports 200 OK.

reported.passage: Send a GET request to /healthz with curl and confirm the status line reports 200 OK.
reported.note: Section 1 asks the learner to send a GET request with curl before the lesson teaches how to use curl.

coursePlan.title: Safe Methods
ideas: GET does not mutate server state

blocks.title: Safe Methods
blocks.body: HTTP GET is a safe method: it retrieves a representation without modifying server state.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately describes HTTP GET?
options: GET retrieves a representation without modifying server state.
GET permanently deletes the target resource on every request.
rationales: Correct: GET is defined as a safe, read-only retrieval method.
Incorrect: GET does not delete resources.
questions.explanation: GET is a safe method that retrieves a representation without mutating server state.

reported.passage: GET permanently deletes the target resource on every request.
reported.note: Question 1's second option says GET permanently deletes the target resource, which contradicts Section 1 saying GET does not modify server state.
